newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees humanitarian disaster ahead in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees humanitarian disaster ahead in Zaire.

text.p: The United States agreed with aid agencies on Wednesday that a humanitarian disaster loomed in eastern Zaire and said it would help cope with the consequences.
U.S. officials said they were still struggling -- but making progress -- with efforts to put together an all-African force of up to 10,000 troops that could react to such crises in the future.

The officials told Reuters that six African countries -- Mali, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Ghana and Tanzania -- have agreed to join the force. At least two others -- Tunisia and Zimbabwe -- are expected to sign up shortly.
Some African countries may provide logistical support or supplies rather than troops, one official said.
Aid agencies in Africa have warned that hundreds of thousands of refugees and local Zaireans fleeing ethnic fighting in eastern Zaire are threatened with hunger and epidemics.
They said Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees in camps around Bukavu and a flood of 220,000 refugees and thousands of Zaireans displaced by fighting would go hungry unless food arrived within days.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "We agree that the present, unpredictable situation could lead to massive population displacements, civilian deaths, which have already occurred, more civilian deaths and to humanitarian disaster."

U.S. ambassadors in Zaire and Rwanda have been asked to talk directly to those governments "to appeal to them to do everything possible to diffuse the current political tension that has arisen because of the fighting in Eastern Zaire," he told reporters.
While it was clear a major disaster loomed, the situation in eastern Zaire remained confused and many of the figures about fleeing refugees could not be verified, he said.

"We will cooperate in any way that the UNHRC (United Nations High Commissoner for Refugees) and the ICRC (International Committee of the Red Cross) requests to help them to cope with the humanitarian consequences of the current fighting and of the refugee flow," Burns added.

A major focus of U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's Africa trip two weeks ago was to rally support among African leaders for the proposed all-Africa force. Reaction was mixed, although he did get some commitments of support.
The force was originally conceived as a way to respond should the fighting in Burundi escalate into genocide as it did in Rwanda in 1994.

But Christopher said the force would be kept ready for deployment in any potential crisis, including possibly some outside of Africa. The aim was not to intervene between warring parties but to meet humanitarian needs of civilians.

Burns said the administration was eager to get the force "going fairly soon ... So it's something that we are planning and we are hopeful about, and I think we do have widespread support in Africa ... The idea is taking root."
The United States is taking the lead in organising, training and equiping the force, which is expected to cost $40 million. Deployment would be extra.
Heeding African concerns, Washington has stipulated that the United Nations would control and deploy such a force, with African nations playing a major decision-making role.
In addition to the African countries, the United States has asked Europeans to participate through financing. So far, Canada, Britain, Ireland and Belgium have agreed to do so, U.S. officials said.
